title: No. 85 — Concluding Remarks (Hamilton)
paragraphs: According to the formal division of the subject announced in my first number, two points would still seem to remain for discussion: "the analogy of the proposed government to your own State constitution," and "the additional security which its adoption will afford to republican government, to liberty, and to property." But these heads have been so fully anticipated and exhausted as the work went on that it would now hardly be possible to do more than repeat, at greater length, what has already been said. The advanced stage of the question and the time already spent on it both forbid that.

It is remarkable that the resemblance between the plan of the Convention and the act that organizes the government of this State holds as much for many of the supposed defects as for the real excellences of the former. Among the pretended defects are that the Executive may be re-elected, that there is no council, that there is no formal bill of rights, and that there is no provision about the liberty of the press. These and several others that have been noted in the course of our inquiries are as much chargeable to the existing constitution of this State as to the one proposed for the Union. A man must have slender claims to consistency if he can rail at the latter for imperfections that he has no difficulty excusing in the former. Indeed there can be no better proof of the insincerity and affectation of some of the zealous adversaries of the plan of the Convention among us, who profess to be devoted admirers of the government under which they live, than the fury with which they have attacked that plan for matters on which our own constitution is equally or perhaps more open to attack.

The additional securities to republican government, to liberty and to property that will come from adopting the plan under consideration consist chiefly in the following. First, the restraints that preserving the Union will place on local factions and insurrections, and on the ambition of powerful individuals in single States, who may gain enough credit and influence from leaders and favorites to become the despots of the people. Second, the reduced opportunities for foreign intrigue, which the dissolution of the Confederacy would invite and make easy. Third, the prevention of large military establishments, which could not fail to grow out of wars between the States in a disunited situation. Fourth, the express guaranty of a republican form of government to each State. Fifth, the absolute and universal exclusion of titles of nobility. And sixth, the precautions against any repetition of those practices by the State governments which have undermined the foundations of property and credit, have planted mutual distrust in the hearts of all classes of citizens, and have brought about an almost universal collapse of morals.

Thus, fellow citizens, I have carried out the task I set myself; with what success, your conduct must determine. I trust at least that you will admit I have not failed in the assurance I gave you about the spirit in which my efforts would be conducted. I have addressed myself purely to your judgment, and I have carefully avoided those harsh attacks which too often disgrace political disputants of every party, and which have been provoked in no small degree by the language and conduct of the opponents of the Constitution. The charge of a conspiracy against the liberties of the people, which has been brought indiscriminately against the advocates of the plan, is too wanton and too malignant not to arouse the indignation of every man who feels in his own heart a refutation of the slander. The perpetual changes rung on the wealthy, the well-born and the great have been such as to disgust all sensible men. And the unwarranted concealments and misrepresentations that have been practiced in various ways to keep the truth from the public eye have been of a kind to demand the condemnation of all honest men. It is not impossible that these circumstances have at times led me into intemperate expressions that I did not intend. It is certain that I have often felt a struggle between feeling and moderation; and if the former has in some instances prevailed, my excuse must be that this has been neither often nor much.

Let us now pause and ask ourselves whether, over the course of these papers, the proposed Constitution has not been satisfactorily defended against the slurs cast on it, and whether it has not been shown to deserve public approval and to be necessary for the public safety and prosperity. Every man is bound to answer these questions to himself as honestly as his conscience and understanding allow, and then to act on the real and sober verdict of his judgment. Nothing can release him from this duty. All the obligations that hold society together call on him, indeed compel him, to carry it out sincerely and honestly. No biased motive, no private interest, no pride in his own opinion, no passing passion or prejudice can justify to himself, to his country or to his descendants a wrong choice of the part he is to play. Let him beware of stubbornly sticking to a party. Let him reflect that what he must decide is not some particular interest of the community but the very existence of the nation. And let him remember that a majority of America has already given its approval to the plan he is now to accept or reject.

I will not conceal that I feel complete confidence in the arguments that recommend the proposed system for your adoption, and that I am unable to see any real force in those by which it has been opposed. I am persuaded that it is the best that our political situation, habits and opinions will allow, and superior to any that the revolution has produced.

Concessions by the friends of the plan that it has no claim to absolute perfection have given its enemies no small cause for triumph. "Why," they say, "should we adopt an imperfect thing? Why not amend it and make it perfect before it is irrevocably established?" This may be plausible enough, but it is only plausible. In the first place, I remark that the extent of these concessions has been greatly exaggerated. They have been presented as amounting to an admission that the plan is radically defective, and that without material alterations the rights and interests of the community cannot safely be entrusted to it. As far as I have understood the meaning of those who make the concessions, this is a complete distortion of their sense. No advocate of the measure can be found who will not declare as his view that the system, though it may not be perfect in every part, is on the whole a good one; that it is the best that the present views and circumstances of the country will permit; and that it is one that promises every kind of security that a reasonable people can desire.

My second answer is that I would count it the height of imprudence to drag out the uncertain state of our national affairs, and to put the Union at risk through one experiment after another, all in a fanciful chase after a perfect plan. I never expect to see a perfect work come from imperfect man. Whatever any collective body decides after deliberation must be a mixture of its members' errors and prejudices as well as their good sense and wisdom. An agreement that is to join thirteen distinct States in a common bond of friendship and union must likewise be a compromise among thirteen dissimilar sets of interests and inclinations. How can perfection come out of such materials?

The reasons given in an excellent little pamphlet recently published in this city(1) are unanswerable in showing the utter improbability of assembling a new convention under circumstances in any degree so favorable to a happy outcome as those in which the recent Convention met, deliberated and concluded. I will not repeat the arguments used there, since I presume the pamphlet itself has circulated widely. It is certainly well worth the reading of every friend of his country. There is, however, one point of view from which the subject of amendments remains to be considered, and in which it has not yet been shown to the public. I cannot bring myself to conclude without first surveying it in this aspect.

It appears to me capable of absolute demonstration that it will be far easier to obtain amendments to the Constitution after it is adopted than before. The moment an alteration is made in the present plan, it becomes, for the purpose of adoption, a new plan, and must undergo a new decision by each State. Its complete establishment throughout the Union will therefore require the concurrence of thirteen States. If, on the contrary, the proposed Constitution is once ratified by all the States as it stands, alterations in it may be made at any time by nine States. Here, then, the chances are as thirteen to nine(2) in favor of later amendment rather than of the original adoption of an entire system.

There is more. Any Constitution for the United States must unavoidably contain a great variety of particulars, and in them thirteen independent States must each be satisfied, either in their interests or in what they believe their interests to be. In any body of men charged with first drafting it, we can naturally expect very different alignments on different points. Many who form a majority on one question will find themselves in the minority on a second, and a different coalition from either will form the majority on a third. So all the particulars that are to make up the whole must be shaped and fitted together in a way that satisfies every party to the compact. And so the difficulties and risks of winning the collective assent to a final act multiply enormously. That multiplication must plainly grow with the number of particulars and the number of parties.

But every amendment to the Constitution, once it was established, would be a single proposition and could be brought forward singly. There would then be no need for maneuvering or compromise on any other point, no giving or taking. The will of the required number would bring the matter at once to a decisive conclusion. Consequently, whenever nine, or rather ten, States were united in wanting a particular amendment, that amendment must infallibly take place. There can be no comparison, therefore, between the ease of making an amendment and that of establishing a complete Constitution in the first instance.

Against the probability of later amendments, it has been argued that the persons delegated to administer the national government will always be unwilling to give up any part of the authority they once possessed. For my own part, I acknowledge a thorough conviction that any amendments that may be thought useful after mature consideration will concern the organization of the government, not the mass of its powers; and on that account alone I think the observation just stated has no weight. I also think it has little weight on another account. The intrinsic difficulty of governing THIRTEEN STATES at all, apart from any calculation based on an ordinary degree of public spirit and integrity, will in my opinion constantly require the national rulers to be accommodating toward the reasonable expectations of their constituents. But there is yet a further consideration, which proves beyond the possibility of a doubt that the observation is futile. It is this: whenever nine States concur, the national rulers will have no choice in the matter. By the fifth article of the plan, Congress will be obliged "on the application of the legislatures of two thirds of the States (which at present amount to nine), to call a convention for proposing amendments, which shall be valid, to all intents and purposes, as part of the Constitution, when ratified by the legislatures of three fourths of the States, or by conventions in three fourths thereof." The words of this article are peremptory. Congress "shall call a convention." Nothing in this respect is left to the discretion of that body. Consequently, all the talk about an unwillingness to change vanishes into air. However difficult it may be supposed to unite two thirds or three fourths of the State legislatures on amendments that may affect local interests, there can be no ground to fear any such difficulty in uniting on points that merely concern the general liberty or security of the people. We may safely rely on the disposition of the State legislatures to erect barriers against the encroachments of the national authority.

If the foregoing argument is a fallacy, I am certainly deceived by it myself; for in my view it is one of those rare instances in which a political truth can be brought to the test of a mathematical demonstration. Those who see the matter in the same light as I do, however zealous they may be for amendments, must agree that adopting the Constitution first is the proper course, as the most direct road to their own object.

Anyone who is willing to accept the truth of the following observations, by a writer as sound as he is ingenious, must lose his eagerness to attempt amendments before the Constitution is established: "To balance a large state or society (says he), whether monarchical or republican, on general laws, is a work of so great difficulty, that no human genius, however comprehensive, is able, by the mere dint of reason and reflection, to effect it. The judgments of many must unite in the work; EXPERIENCE must guide their labor; TIME must bring it to perfection, and the FEELING of inconveniences must correct the mistakes which they inevitably fall into in their first trials and experiments."(3) These wise reflections teach moderation to all sincere lovers of the Union. They ought to warn them against gambling with anarchy, civil war, a permanent estrangement of the States from one another, and perhaps the military despotism of a victorious demagogue, in pursuit of something they are unlikely to get except from TIME and EXPERIENCE. It may be a failing of political courage in me, but I admit that I cannot be as untroubled as those who pretend that the dangers of staying longer in our present situation are imaginary. A NATION, without a NATIONAL GOVERNMENT, is, to my mind, an awful sight. Establishing a Constitution in a time of profound peace, by the voluntary consent of a whole people, is a PRODIGY, and I look forward to seeing it completed with trembling anxiety. No rule of prudence can justify releasing the hold we now have, in so difficult an undertaking, on seven of the thirteen States, or starting the course over again after covering so large a part of the ground. I dread new attempts all the more because I know that POWERFUL INDIVIDUALS, in this State and in others, are enemies to a general national government in every possible form.
1. Entitled "An Address to the People of the State of New York."
2. It would be more accurate to say TEN, because although two thirds can start the measure, three fourths must ratify it.
3. Hume's Essays, Vol. I, p. 128: "The Rise of Arts and Sciences."
